content: Progressive muscle weakness is a primary symptom observed in most hereditary and acquired muscle diseases. Creatine supplementation has been shown to enhance muscle performance in healthy individuals. This review is an update of the 2007 Cochrane review that assessed the effects of creatine treatment in muscle disorders, with prior updates conducted in 2009 and 2011. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of creatine compared to placebo in addressing muscle weakness associated with muscle diseases. A comprehensive search for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted on September 11, 2012, using databases such as the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. The search included studies from January 1966 to September 2012 for MEDLINE and from January 1980 to September 2012 for EMBASE. The inclusion criteria focused on RCTs or quasi-RCTs that compared creatine treatment to placebo in individuals with hereditary muscle diseases or idiopathic inflammatory myopathies. Two independent reviewers applied the selection criteria, assessed the quality of the trials, and extracted data. Missing data were obtained directly from the investigators. A total of 14 trials, involving 364 randomized participants, met the inclusion criteria. Most studies demonstrated a low risk of bias, although one trial exhibited a high risk of selection, performance, and detection bias. No new studies were identified in this update. Meta-analysis of six trials involving 192 participants with muscular dystrophies showed a significant improvement in muscle strength in the creatine group compared to the placebo group. The mean difference in muscle strength was 8.47% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.55 to 13.38). Additionally, pooled data from four trials with 115 participants revealed that a significantly higher number of participants reported feeling better during creatine treatment compared to placebo, with a risk ratio of 4.51 (95% CI: 2.33 to 8.74). One trial involving 37 participants with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies demonstrated a significant improvement in functional performance with creatine treatment. Importantly, no trial reported any clinically relevant adverse events associated with creatine use. In metabolic myopathies, meta-analyses of three cross-over trials involving 33 participants did not show a significant difference in muscle strength between the creatine and placebo groups. However, one trial reported a significant decline in activities of daily living (mean difference: 0.54 on a 1 to 10 scale; 95% CI: 0.14 to 0.93) and an increase in muscle pain during high-dose creatine treatment in individuals with McArdle disease. In conclusion, high-quality evidence from RCTs indicates that shortand medium-term creatine treatment improves muscle strength in individuals with muscular dystrophies. There is also evidence supporting improved functional performance in muscular dystrophy and idiopathic inflammatory myopathy. Creatine is generally well tolerated in these populations. However, high-quality but limited evidence does not support significant improvements in muscle strength in metabolic myopathies. Furthermore, high-dose creatine treatment may impair daily activities and increase muscle pain in individuals with McArdle disease.
